自古帝王必有訓典以貽天下後世。至我則有《大誥三編》；在帝則有《為善陰隲》、《孝順事實》；在□有《五倫書》，皆萬世之大訓也。比早□壹萬國之幅員，兼百代之文獻，邇鉅細翕然可指，廢興善惡炳然可，時曰儒臣所輯，而親定其綱，□雄冠于首，其可與前四書同垂于萬世歟？竊嘗伏觀其畧，自兩京暨十三布政司，皆首圖而次志。圖則郡縣碁布，志則山川、風俗、人物、名宦之屬，綱舉目張，
translation_en:
Third Session

Policy Questions

Since antiquity, emperors and kings have always had instructional canons to bequeath to the realm and to posterity. Coming to Our [Grand Progenitor], there were the Three Compilations of the Grand Pronouncements (Dagao sanbian); in the time of the [Filial and Cultured] Emperor, there were the Secret Blessings for Doing Good (Weishan yinzhi) and the True Examples of Filial Piety and Obedience (Xiaoshun shishi); and in the time of [Emperor Xuanzong][?], there was the Book of the Five Human Relationships (Wulun shu)—all of which are great instructions for ten thousand generations. More recently, [when the late Emperor composed the Comprehensive Gazetteer of the Great Ming][?], it unified the territories of ten thousand states and encompassed the documentary heritage of a hundred generations. [Regions far and] near, matters great and small, can all be pointed to at once; rise and fall, good and evil, can be clearly [examined]. Although it is said to have been compiled by Confucian officials, [His Majesty] personally determined its guiding framework, and [his imperial preface] stands majestically at its head. Can it not be handed down to ten thousand generations alongside the aforementioned four books? I have humbly examined its general outline: from the Two Capitals down to the thirteen Provincial Administration Commissions, every section begins with maps and follows with treatises. In the maps, prefectures and counties are arrayed like pieces on a game board; in the treatises, mountains and rivers, local customs, notable figures, famous officials, and the like are set forth with the main cord drawn and every mesh opened, …

眡如也。夫談今者必證古，舉遠者必先近。圖之與志，兩京與十三布政司之制，在古亦有之乎？山川以下在布政司者，固博乎難以議為也；其在南畿者，諸生之所見聞，可舉其尤歟？且羲卦禹疇，異書也，尚相表裏，况我□相表裏者乎？堯言萬世如見，皇上真敬對無忽。

天下未甞亡，惟託於人□絕，故其行於世者有明有晦，□天命之所為，非人知力之所能及也。論者謂：堯、舜、禹、湯、文、武、周公生而道始行，孔子、孟子生而道始明。前此三皇繼天立極，何云至是始行歟？帝王於道未始不明，何云至是始明歟？有謂「天不生仲尼，萬古如長夜」，何人有此的見歟？有謂「使孔、孟同時，將並駕其說於天下」，
translation_en:
…clearly visible before one's eyes. Now, those who discuss the present must verify it against antiquity, and those who cite what is distant must begin with what is near. Did the use of both maps and treatises, and the system of the Two Capitals and the Thirteen Provincial Administration Commissions, also exist in antiquity? As for the mountains, rivers, and subsequent categories within the Provincial Administration Commissions, they are indeed so vast as to be difficult to discuss thoroughly; yet as for those within the Southern Metropolitan Area (Nanji), which you students have seen and heard of yourselves, can you cite the most notable among them? Moreover, the trigrams of Fuxi and the "Nine Categories" of Yu are from different works, yet they still complement one another as exterior and interior—how much more so [the works of] our [Dynasty?] [?] that complement one another as exterior and interior! The words of Yao are as if seen across ten thousand generations; [may you] respond with genuine reverence for His Majesty [?] and without negligence.

…[The Way in] the world has never perished; it is only that as its transmission through men [is sustained or] broken off [?], its practice in the world has periods of clarity and obscurity. [Whether it is practiced or obscured is] wrought by the Mandate of Heaven, and is not something that human knowledge and strength can attain. Commentators say that only with the birth of Yao, Shun, Yu, Tang, King Wen, King Wu, and the Duke of Zhou did the Way begin to be practiced, and only with the birth of Confucius and Mencius did the Way begin to be illuminated. Prior to this, the Three Sovereigns succeeded Heaven and established the standard—why then say that only at this point did it begin to be practiced? The emperors and kings were never unilluminated regarding the Way—why then say that only at this point did it begin to be illuminated? Someone has said, "Had Heaven not given birth to Zhongni [Confucius], ten thousand ages would have been like an endless night"—who possessed such definitive insight? And someone has said, "Had Confucius and Mencius lived at the same time, they would have driven their doctrines side by side throughout the world"…

title: 成化七年應天府鄉試錄
text:
此果定論歟有謂秦漢以下諸儒說道
理直是說夢若晁錯田生申公高堂生
鄭玄王肅孔穎達之徒宜乎其然矣然
則董子揚子文中子世稱名儒其亦見
道之未真歟又謂只有韓文公說得畧
□歟又有謂孔孟之道周程張
□□之道朱子又繼之朱
歟其所繼者何歟
===
□續既晦而復明端在於今
日也諸士子應賓興而來行且觀
□之光將何道以輔
文明之治願紬繹以對
問余讀易至于豐之繇未嘗不嘆聖人之
為世慮深且至也夫世之所憂者屯耳

之道朱子又繼之朱
歟其所繼者何歟
===
往續既晦而復明端在於今
日也諸士子應賓興而來行且觀
之光將何道以輔
文明之治願紬繹以對
問余讀易至于豐之繇未嘗不嘆聖人之
為世慮深且至也夫世之所憂者屯耳
punctuated:
此果定論歟？有謂秦、漢以下諸儒說道理，直是說夢。若晁錯、田生、申公、高堂生、鄭玄、王肅、孔穎達之徒，宜乎其然矣；然則董子、揚子、文中子，世稱名儒，其亦見道之未真歟？又謂只有韓文公說得畧□歟？又有謂孔、孟之道，周、程、張□□之道，朱子又繼之。朱歟？其所繼者何歟？□續既晦而復明，端在於今日也。諸士子應賓興而來，行且觀□之光，將何道以輔文明之治？願紬繹以對。

問：余讀《易》至于〈豐〉之繇，未嘗不嘆聖人之為世慮深且至也。夫世之所憂者，屯耳、
translation_en:
…Is this truly a definitive judgment? There is a saying that when the various scholars from the Qin and Han dynasties onward spoke of moral principles, it was simply like talking in a dream. As for the likes of Chao Cuo 晁錯, Master Tian 田生, Master Shen 申公, Master Gaotang 高堂生, Zheng Xuan 鄭玄, Wang Su 王肅, and Kong Yingda 孔穎達, it is fitting that it was so; yet if that is the case, did Master Dong 董子 (Dong Zhongshu 董仲舒), Master Yang 揚子 (Yang Xiong 揚雄), and Master Wenzhong 文中子 (Wang Tong 王通), whom the world calls renowned scholars, also fail to see the true nature of the Way? It is further said that only Han Wengong 韓文公 (Han Yu 韓愈) spoke of it somewhat […?] And it is also said that the Way of Confucius and Mencius was [carried on by?] Zhou 周 (Zhou Dunyi 周敦頤), the Chengs 程 (Cheng Hao 程顥 and Cheng Yi 程頤), and Zhang 張 (Zhang Zai 張載), and [their] Way was in turn succeeded by Master Zhu 朱子 (Zhu Xi 朱熹). [Was it completed in Master?] Zhu? What was it that they succeeded to? […] continuing it so that after being obscured it is made bright again truly lies in the present day. You gentlemen have come in response to the call for the recommendation of the worthy, and are soon to behold the glory of [the realm]; by what Way will you assist the enlightened governance of our civilization? I wish for you to draw out your thoughts and reply in full.

Question: Whenever I read the Book of Changes (Yi 易) down to the judgment on the hexagram "Abundance" (Feng 豐), I never fail to sigh in admiration at how deep and thorough the sages' concern for the world was. Now, what the world worries about are "Difficulty at the Beginning" (Zhun 屯), …

title: 成化七年應天府鄉試錄
text:
否耳蹇耳剝耳幸而豐焉世所樂也而
聖人廼謂其可憂援日月之中具盈食
以為喻必欲王者尚大而照天下斯可
無虞其為世慮何其深且至耶今天下
昇平百年犁鋤尋於遐徼雞犬囂於窮
□□人墻屋被文繡而婢僕厭粱
□□□豐矣自
□□□藩省如雨內外之閑廐
□□□□□□矣文臣鱗稡壅
===
□□□□□□弗能給皆患無術
□□□□豐矣普天率土凡百
□□□唐宋之盛弗能踰也然民
□□有水旱則窮者流亡富者
乏匱兵馬豐矣而一有征伐則精卒勁
騎俱不給於營陣人材豐矣而庶官之
負恒闕緩急輒有乏材之嘆其故何也
豐之可憂者其謂此耶非耶抑又有大
於此者耶天下之可憂者其詳有幾憂

否耳聾耳刵耳幸而豐焉世所樂也而
聖人迺謂其可憂援日月之中昃盈食
以爲喻必欲王者尚大而照天下斯可
無虞其爲世慮何其深且至耶今天下
承平百年犁鋤尋於遐僻雞犬囂於窮
谷人墻屋被文繡而婢僕厭粱
豐矣自
御宮〔省如雨內外之閑廄〕〔奚文尋鱗崪壅〕
===
之匱兵馬豐矣而一有征伐則精卒勁
騎俱不給於營陣人材豐矣而庶官之
負恒闕緩急輙有乏材之嘆其故何也
豐之可憂者其謂此耶非耶抑又有大
於此者耶天下之可憂者其詳有幾憂
〔有水旱則窮者流亡富者〕
〔唐宋之盛弗能踰也然民〕
〔言豐矣普天率土凡百〕
〔弗能給皆患無術〕
punctuated: 否耳、蹇耳、剝耳，幸而豐焉，世所樂也，而聖人廼謂其可憂，援日月之中具盈食以為喻，必欲王者尚大而照天下，斯可無虞，其為世慮何其深且至耶！今天下昇平百年，犁鋤尋於遐徼，雞犬囂於窮□□，人墻屋被文繡，而婢僕厭粱□□，□豐矣；自□□□藩省如雨，內外之閑廐□□□□，□□矣；文臣鱗稡，壅□□□□□□弗能給，皆患無術□□，□□豐矣。普天率土，凡百□□，□唐、宋之盛弗能踰也。然民□□有水旱，則窮者流亡，富者乏匱；兵馬豐矣，而一有征伐，則精卒勁騎俱不給於營陣；人材豐矣，而庶官之負恒闕，緩急輒有乏材之嘆，其故何也？豐之可憂者，其謂此耶？非耶？抑又有大於此者耶？天下之可憂者，其詳有幾？憂
translation_en:
… Obstruction (Pi), Limping (Jian), and Peeling (Bo). When by good fortune there is Abundance (Feng), it is what the world rejoices in; yet the Sage nevertheless said that it is a cause for worry. Drawing on the metaphor of the sun at midday and the moon at full, which are bound to decline and eclipse, he insisted that a true king must prize greatness and illuminate all under Heaven, for only then can there be no cause for anxiety. How deep and thorough was his concern for the world!

Today, all under Heaven has enjoyed peace and prosperity for a hundred years. Plows and hoes are regularly plied on the distant frontiers; chickens and dogs clamor in remote [villages?]; [rich?] men's walls and houses are draped in patterned embroidery, while maids and servants have their fill of fine grain [and meat—thus the people?] are abundant indeed. From [the capital out to?] the provinces, [troops are massed] like rain, and the corrals and stables inside and outside the capital [are filled to capacity—thus soldiers and horses are abundant?] indeed. Civil officials are gathered thick as fish scales, crowding [the ministries so that positions?] cannot suffice to accommodate them, and all worry about lacking a way [to place them—thus talents?] are abundant indeed. Beneath the whole sky and to the borders of the land, in all [things], [even] the flourishing eras of the Tang and Song could not surpass this.

Yet although the people [are abundant, once] there is flood or drought, the poor flee as refugees and the rich fall into want. Soldiers and horses are abundant, yet once there is a military campaign, elite foot soldiers and strong cavalry are alike insufficient for the camps and battle formations. Men of talent are abundant, yet the quotas of the various offices are constantly short, and in times of urgency there is always the lament of a dearth of talent. Why is this so? When Abundance is said to be a cause for worry, does it refer to this, or not? Or is there something even greater than this? How many specific causes for worry are there in the world? To worry…

title: 成化七年應天府鄉試錄
text:
而圖之計將安出凡天下之事與其貽
悔於後孰若預憂於先前數者預憂而
為之計則可以保豐於悠久否則能無
悔乎今
聖天子臨御正如日中之照天下有司欲秉炬
以佐其光也故咨於諸生范文正公有
言當先天下之憂而憂後天下之樂
諸生豈無憂天下如文正者乎其
言
===
人三才也三才之道有天下者所
理焉古者作蓋天以定氣敬乎天
制莫善於羲和之造璣衡仰觀以
齊七政作曆以授人時即渾天儀也厥
後或經營之量度之鑄銅為之儀象又
有為內外之儀曰六合曰三辰曰四遊
其法制果沿於古乎抑有所增損乎古
者畫野分州經土設井因乎地矣然功
莫盛於神禹之平水土成五服以封建
alt_text:
而圖之計將安出凡天下之事與其貽
悔於後孰若預憂於先前數者預憂而
爲之計則可以保豐於悠久否則能無
悔乎今
聖天子臨御正如日中之照天下有司欲秉烜
以佐其光也故咨於諸生范文正公有
當先天下之憂而憂後天下之樂
諸生豈無憂天下如文正者乎其
台
===
入三才也三才之道有天下者所
埋焉古者作盖天以定氣敬乎天
制莫善於羲和之造璣衡仰觀以
政作曆以授人時即渾天儀也歟
後戓經營之量度之鑄銅爲之儀象又
有爲内外之儀曰六合曰三辰曰四遊
其法制果沿於古乎抑有所增損乎古
者畫野分州經土設井因乎地矣然功
莫盛於神禹之平水土成五服以封建
punctuated:
而圖之，計將安出？凡天下之事，與其貽悔於後，孰若預憂於先？前數者，預憂而為之計，則可以保豐於悠久；否則，能無悔乎？今聖天子臨御，正如日中之照天下，有司欲秉炬以佐其光也，故咨於諸生。范文正公有言：「當先天下之憂而憂，後天下之樂。」諸生豈無憂天下如文正者乎？其言。
人，三才也。三才之道，有天下者所理焉。古者作蓋天以定氣，敬乎天，制莫善於羲和之造璣衡，仰觀以齊七政，作曆以授人時，即渾天儀也。厥後或經營之，量度之，鑄銅為之儀象；又有為內外之儀，曰六合、曰三辰、曰四遊。其法制果沿於古乎？抑有所增損乎？古者畫野分州，經土設井，因乎地矣。然功莫盛於神禹之平水土，成五服以封建，
translation_en:
…and plan for them, from where will the strategies come? In all affairs of the realm, rather than leaving regrets for later, how could that compare to worrying about them in advance? If for the several matters mentioned above we worry in advance and formulate plans for them, then we can preserve Abundance (Feng) for a long time to come; otherwise, how could we avoid regret? Today the Sacred Son of Heaven reigns, just like the sun at midday illuminating all under heaven, and the authorities wish to hold up torches to assist His light; therefore we consult you students. Master Fan Wenzheng (Fan Zhong淹) had a saying: "One ought to worry before the world worries, and rejoice after the world rejoices […]." Among you students, how could there be none who worry for the world like Wenzheng? State your views […].

[Heaven, Earth, and] Man are the Three Powers (sancai). The Way of the Three Powers is what he who possesses all under heaven [attends to and] orders. In antiquity, they devised the Canopy Heaven (gaitian) model to determine the seasonal vital breaths, thus showing reverence for Heaven; yet no system was more excellent than Xi and He's construction of the sighting tube and rotating sphere (jiheng), looking up to observe and thereby align the Seven Regulators (qizheng), and making calendars to grant the seasons to the people—which is namely the celestial sphere (huntian yi). Thereafter, some planned and measured it, casting bronze to make astronomical instruments and effigies; and there were also those who made inner and outer rings, called the Six Conjunctions (liuhe), the Three Luminaries (sanchen), and the Four Roamers (siyou). Did their methods and systems truly follow antiquity, or did they add to or subtract from them? In antiquity, they demarcated the wilds and divided the provinces, laid out the land and established the well-field system, thus adapting to the Earth. Yet no achievement was more flourishing than Divine Yu's pacification of the waters and lands, establishing the Five Domains (wufu) for enfeoffment, …

title: 成化七年應天府鄉試錄
text:
則三壤以井田詳于禹貢也継是或郊
□鄙之辨土以任土事又有分天
□十三部為十道為十五路其
□□古乎抑各因其形勢乎禮
隆古不宜有詳畧之異何
而略於政王者詳於政而
樂之從先進夫子也然愛
是崇本原器數之咸備其得
以仁義為本先王也然鞭
□寬嚴踈密之兼致其幾
□□人所以理三才者果出於
□□因其自然歟其亦有所為歟
亦足以致治歟諸生生長首
善
□□之道追配古昔之盛必講之
□為我一陳之
問人心不同有如其面行治所由異也古

則三壤以井田詳于禹貢也繼是或郊
鄙之辨土以任土事又有分天
下十三部爲十道爲十五路其
於古乎抑各因其形勢乎禮
隆古不宜有詳畧之異何

樂之從先進夫子也然愛
是崇本原器數之咸備其得
以仁義爲本先王也然鞭
===
免寛嚴莊容之兼致其幾
聖人所以理三才者果出於
因其自然歟其亦有所爲歟
亦足以致治歟諸生生長首
□
之道追配古昔之盛必講之
爲我一陳之
問人心不同有如其面行治所由異也古
punctuated:
則三壤以井田，詳于《禹貢》也。継是或郊□鄙之，辨土以任土事；又有分天□十三部、為十道、為十五路。其□□古乎？抑各因其形勢乎？禮隆古，不宜有詳畧之異，何而略於政，王者詳於政而樂之從先進，夫子也；然愛是崇，本原器數之咸備，其得以仁義為本，先王也；然鞭□寬嚴踈密之兼致，其幾□□人所以理三才者，果出於□□因其自然歟？其亦有所為歟？亦足以致治歟？諸生生長首善，□□之道，追配古昔之盛，必講之□，為我一陳之。
問：人心不同，有如其面，行治所由異也。古
translation_en:
… and graded the three classes of soil to establish the well-field system, as set forth in detail in the Tribute of Yu (Yu gong). Following this, some demarcated the suburbs, [regions?], and outlying districts, distinguishing the soils in order to assign land duties; others divided the [realm into] thirteen regions, ten circuits, or fifteen circuits. Did their [institutions follow] antiquity, or were they each adapted to the topography of the land? Rites and [music] reached their height in antiquity and ought not to have differed in degree of detail or simplicity; why is it that [the Emperors were detailed in ceremonial?] and summary in governance, whereas the Kings were detailed in governance and [summary in ceremonial?]. In rites and music, to follow the men of former times was the principle of the Master [Confucius]; yet in cherishing [the ceremonial sheep] and honoring [the caps of Yin and chariot of Zhou?], with both fundamental principles and ritual vessels and numbers fully provided, wherein lay the gain [or loss?]. Taking benevolence and righteousness as the foundation was the way of the Former Kings; yet the whip [and bamboo] were also used, combining leniency and severity, looseness and strictness—what was the subtle mechanism behind this? [That] whereby the [ancients?] ordered the Three Powers [Heaven, Earth, and Man]—did it truly issue from [a single source?], following what is natural, or did it also involve deliberate human effort? And was [the governance of later ages?] also sufficient to bring about order? You students, born and raised in the premier place of moral transformation [the capital], must have thoroughly discussed the way of [the present dynasty?] in matching the flourishing of antiquity. Set it all forth for me.

Question: Men's minds differ just as their faces do, and from this arise differences in conduct and governance. Among the men of antiquity…

title: 成化七年應天府鄉試錄
text:
之人若堯桀凱凶較然霄壤天下萬世
所知矣若夫聖之清和伯主之正譎大
夫之濫隘士之拯溺受牛與贖人辭金
拒隣之嫠與嫗不逮門之女孔孟有定
他若相之或通或介將之或寬或
刑之或恕或刻以至立教之或以
以剛克守郡者或以術破奸黨
寇讐治邑者或戴星而勞或
典選者或嗔而與人官或笑
人官治兵者或不戮一人或鞭
三人耳至於同仕宦也有苦身
有放意自恣同奏事也有力爭有
□□同侍講也有為元老而恭有起布
□莊同為直指使也有多誅殺有多
使秦也有專美本朝有微說國
弊同致師也有右入壘有左射以菆同
在軍見君使也有納不納者矣同除喪
鼓琴也有和不和者矣同鋤地見金也

之人若堯舜禹湯文武周公孔子較然霄壤天下萬世
所知矣若夫聖之清和伯夷柳下惠之正譎大
夫之濫隘士之拯溺受牛與贖人辭金
垣隣之婺與嫗不建門之女孔孟有定
他若相之或通或介將之或寬或
刑之或恕或刻以至立教之或以
以剛克守郡者或以術破奸黨
寇讐治邑者或戴星而勞或
與選者或嗔而與人官或笑
===
人官治兵者或不戮一人或鞭
三人耳至於同仕宦也有苦身
有放意自恣同奏事也有力爭有
有同侍講也有為元老而恭有起布
從同為直指使也有多誅殺有多
使秦也有專美本朝有徽說國
弊同致師也有右入壘有左射以蔵同
在軍見君使也有納不納者矣同除喪
鼓琴也有和不和者矣同鋤地見金也
punctuated: 之人，若堯、桀、凱、凶，較然霄壤，天下萬世所知矣。若夫聖之清、和，伯主之正、譎，大夫之濫、隘，士之拯溺受牛與贖人辭金，拒隣之嫠與嫗不逮門之女，孔、孟有定，他若相之或通或介，將之或寬或刑之或恕或刻，以至立教之或以以剛克，守郡者或以術破奸黨寇讐，治邑者或戴星而勞，或典選者或嗔而與人官，或笑人官，治兵者或不戮一人，或鞭三人耳。至於同仕宦也，有苦身有放意自恣；同奏事也，有力爭有□□；同侍講也，有為元老而恭，有起布□莊；同為直指使也，有多誅殺，有多使秦也，有專美本朝，有微說國弊；同致師也，有右入壘，有左射以菆；同在軍見君使也，有納不納者矣；同除喪鼓琴也，有和不和者矣；同鋤地見金也，
translation_en:
… the ancients—such as Yao and Jie, or the Eight Harmonious Ones (Bakai) and the Four Fiends (Sixiong)—are as distinctly different as heaven and earth, as is known to all under heaven for ten thousand generations. As for the purity and harmony of sages [Boyi and Liuxia Hui], the uprightness and craftiness of hegemonic lords [Duke Wen of Jin and Duke Huan of Qi], the laxity and narrowness of grand masters [Zang Wenzhong and Liuxia Hui], the scholars who rescued a drowning man and accepted an ox [Zigong's contrast: Zilu] versus the one who ransomed a man and declined the reward money [Zigong], and the man who refused a neighboring widow versus the one who sheltered a woman who could not reach her door in time [Liuxia Hui]—on these, Confucius and Mencius had settled judgments [missing char: 論].

As for others: chief ministers who were either accommodating or uncompromising [e.g. Xiao He / Cao Can or姚崇 / 宋璟]; generals who were either lenient or [missing chars: 嚴, 司] administrators of punishment who were either forgiving or harsh; down to those who established teaching either by [missing chars: 寬容, 或] overcoming through firmness; commandery governors who either used stratagems to break up treacherous factions [missing chars: 或視民如] or enemies; district magistrates who either toiled under the stars [Zijian's contrast: Wuma Qi] or [missing chars: 彈琴而治]; directors of selection who either granted offices in anger or laughed [missing chars: 而不與] people offices; and commanders of troops who either executed not a single man or whipped [missing chars: 背日斬] three men only.

Furthermore, among those who equally served in office, some afflicted their own bodies [with frugality], while others indulged themselves at will; among those who equally presented memorials, some contended forcefully, while others [2 illegible chars]; among those who equally served as Expositors-in-Waiting, some were elder statesmen and yet reverent, while others rose from commoner status [1 illegible char: 而] and were dignified; among those who equally served as Direct-Pointing Envoys (zhizhi shi), some carried out many executions, while others had many [missing chars: 平反; 同] who were sent as envoys to Qin, some exclusively praised their own court, while others subtly spoke of their state's flaws; among those who equally challenged the enemy to battle, some entered the ramparts from the right, while others shot from the left with fine arrows; among those who equally received their ruler's envoy while in the army, some admitted him and some did not; among those who equally played the zither upon completing mourning, some produced harmonious sounds and some did not; among those who equally saw gold while hoeing the ground, …

title: 成化七年應天府鄉試錄
text:
有擲不擲者矣若此者孰優孰劣疇是
疇非九原可作其誰與歸夫論別人物
者大學格致之一端也毋徒諉諸不暇
alt_text:
有擲不擲者矣若此者孰優孰劣疇是
疇非九原可作其誰與歸夫論別人物
者大學格致之一端也毋徒諉諸不暇
punctuated: 有擲不擲者矣。若此者，孰優孰劣？疇是疇非？九原可作，其誰與歸？夫論別人物者，大學格致之一端也，毋徒諉諸不暇。
translation_en: … there were those who cast it away and those who did not. In cases such as these, who was superior and who was inferior? Who was right and who was wrong? If they could be raised from the Nine Springs, with whom would one align oneself? Now, evaluating and distinguishing historical figures is one aspect of the investigation of things and the extension of knowledge in the Great Learning (Daxue); do not merely excuse yourselves by claiming a lack of leisure.

translation_en:
First Session
Expositions on the Four Books

"What is meant by 'making the thoughts sincere' is allowing no self-deception, as when we hate a bad smell, or as when we love what is beautiful. This is called self-satisfaction. Therefore, the superior man must be watchful over himself when he is alone. There is no evil to which the petty man, dwelling retired, will not proceed, but when he sees a superior man, he instantly tries to disguise himself, concealing his evil, and displaying what is good. The other beholds him, as if he saw his heart and reins; of what use is his disguise? This is an instance of the saying—'What truly is within will be manifested without.' Therefore, the superior man must be watchful over himself when he is alone. The disciple Zeng said, 'What ten eyes behold, what ten hands point to, is to be regarded with reverence!' Riches adorn a house, and virtue adorns the person. The mind is expanded, and the body is at ease. Therefore, the superior man must make his thoughts sincere."

為文尤難場中如此作者鮮矣
大學釋誠意之詳無非戒人自欺而勉人自慊
也夫誠其意者自脩之首也毋自欺而必自慊
則意誠矣大學得不反覆詳言以示人哉傳者

人知為善以去惡而心之所發有未實是之謂

必得皆以快足於己而不可徇外為人是之謂

That the Great Learning (Daxue 大學) explains "making the thoughts sincere" in such detail is simply to warn people against deceiving themselves and to encourage them to find true satisfaction in themselves. Now, making one's thoughts sincere is the starting point of self-cultivation. When one does not deceive oneself and insists on finding true satisfaction in oneself, one's thoughts become sincere; how, then, could the Great Learning not speak of this repeatedly and in detail to instruct people? The meaning of the commentator is roughly this: What the Classic text calls "making one's thoughts sincere" lies in forbidding oneself to practice self-deception. When a person knows that he should do good in order to rid himself of evil, and yet what issues from his mind is not completely genuine, this is called self-deception. One must genuinely exert one's strength to forbid this, so that in hating evil one is as genuine as in hating a foul odor and strives to cast it off decisively, and in loving good one is as genuine as in loving a beautiful appearance and seeks unfailingly to attain it—doing all this for the contentment and satisfaction of oneself, and never pursuing external appearances for the sake of others. This is called finding satisfaction in oneself. Yet whether one's thoughts are genuine or not is something that others cannot know and that oneself alone knows; therefore the gentleman must be watchful over this in order to examine its subtleincipience. When the petty man dwells in solitude and does evil, there is indeed no limit to how far he will go; yet in his heart he too knows that good ought to be done and evil ought to be cast away. Thus, upon seeing a gentleman, he shrinks back and conceals himself, covering up his real evil and displaying his false goodness. Little does he realize that others already see through his good and evil as clearly as if they were looking straight into his lungs and liver; his evil in the end cannot be covered up, and his goodness in the end cannot be feigned—so what use is there in pretending? This is what is meant by "what is truly within will be manifested without," and therefore the gentleman takes this as a weighty…

title: 成化七年應天府鄉試錄
text:
為戒而必謹其獨也曾子甞謂幽獨之中無一
人指視之者而善惡之不可揜炳然十目所共
視森然十手所共指可畏之甚也人可自欺而
不誠其意乎彼積財成富則能華澤其屋矣積
善成德則能華澤其身矣德之澤身者一心無
愧而廣大寛平四體無累而安舒康泰此則自
慊而意已誠矣是故君子必毋自欺求自慊以
誠其意也傳者兩言慎獨而旨益明三言君子
而意彌切欲誠意者可不詳玩而猛省乎抑甞
===
味之大學之道盖莫要於誠意者矣前乎格致
之理待誠意而行之也後乎正脩齊治平之道
由誠意而進之也故傳者於此獨詳悉而痛切
焉先儒謂此章為大學一篇之要有旨哉

…take this as a warning, and must be watchful over himself when alone. Master Zeng (Zengzi 曾子) once said that in the midst of seclusion and solitude, where there is not a single person pointing or looking on, good and evil cannot be concealed—as brightly manifest as if ten eyes were looking at it together, and as sternly arrayed as if ten hands were pointing at it together. How utterly awe-inspiring! Can a person deceive himself and fail to make his intentions sincere? Now, accumulating wealth to achieve riches can adorn and luster one's house; accumulating goodness to achieve virtue can adorn and luster one's person. When virtue lusters the person, the mind is free of shame, vast, and寬平 (broad and tranquil); the four limbs are free of burden, at ease, and serene. In this way one is satisfied with oneself, and one's intentions have already become sincere. Therefore, the superior man must not deceive himself, and must seek self-satisfaction in order to make his intentions sincere. The commentator twice speaks of being watchful when alone, whereby the meaning becomes ever clearer, and thrice speaks of the superior man, whereby the import becomes ever more earnest. Can anyone who wishes to make his intentions sincere fail to savor this carefully and examine himself vigorously? Moreover, when I have pondered it, in the Way of the Great Learning (Daxue), there is surely nothing more essential than making the intentions sincere. What precedes it—the principles of investigating things and extending knowledge—awaits the sincerity of intentions in order to be put into practice; what follows it—the Way of rectifying the mind, cultivating the person, regulating the family, ordering the state, and bringing peace to the world—proceeds forward from the sincerity of intentions. Thus the commentator is uniquely detailed and incisively earnest on this point. When earlier Confucians called this chapter the essential pivot of the entire Great Learning, how meaningful that was!

本旨非老學不能也

眾皆為近易之道則世自無不治矣夫親親長
長道之近且易者但人皆為是道則世自無不
治矣而可求之遠且難哉今夫天性之親天倫

倫而致其敬無一夫之不長其長矣夫如是天

而傲兄天下所以不平也既人人親親而長長

Examiner and Librarian Yang comments: This essay has passages that awaken and prompt reflection in the reader.

When everyone practices the Way that is near and easy, the world will naturally be completely well-governed. Now, loving one's parents and respecting one's elders are aspects of the Way that are near and easy. Provided that all people practice this Way, the world will naturally be completely well-governed—how then could one seek it in what is distant and difficult? Now, the parents given by one's innate nature and the elders of one's natural human relationships are, for any person, very near at hand; having parents and loving them, or having elders and respecting them, is for any person very easy, and the Way from the beginning does not lie outside of this. If one abandons this and seeks elsewhere, it becomes distant and difficult, and on the contrary one loses it. Provided only that everyone loves their parents and respects their elders, the world will naturally be at peace. Now, all people have parents, yet some fail to love them; if today everyone loves their parents, then both the noble and the humble will all be able to follow their innate nature and extend their affection, and there will not be a single person who does not love their parents. All people have elders, yet some fail to respect them; if today everyone respects their elders, then both the young and the great will all be able to remain mindful of their natural human relationships and extend their reverence, and there will not be a single person who does not respect their elders. When it is like this, how could the world not be at peace? For when people do not all love their parents and respect their elders—going so far as to rebel against their fathers and behave arrogantly toward their elder brothers—that is why the world is not at peace. Once everyone loves their parents and respects their elders, …

Is this not the pacification of the world? Now, since the pacification of the world lies solely in loving one's亲 (parents) and respecting one's elders, how can those who seek the Way abandon loving their parents and respecting their elders to seek it elsewhere? Alas! As for this Way, the foolish and unworthy certainly fail to attain it, while the worthy and wise seek it in what is distant and difficult, and thus also fail to attain it. This is what the sages and worthies deeply worried about. Therefore, after Mencius said in the preceding passage, "The Way lies in what is near, yet people seek it in what is far; the task lies in what is easy, yet people seek it in what is difficult," he spoke these words to follow it up. This was to make the worthy and wise not neglect this Way because it is near and easy, and also to make the foolish and unworthy know that this Way is near and easy so that they might reach it. Is his meaning not profound indeed!

Exposition on the Book of Changes (Yiyi)

"Increase (Yi): diminishing the above to increase the below, the people rejoice without limit. Descending from above to reach below, its Way shines forth greatly. 'It is advantageous to have somewhere to go,' for with centrality and correctness there is blessing. 'It is advantageous to cross the great stream,' for the way of wood thus goes forward. Increase is movement and compliance, advancing daily without limit. Heaven bestows and Earth generates; its increase knows no bounds. All the ways of Increase proceed in keeping with the time."

Jiang Tinggui 蔣廷貴

Comment by Associate Examiner Instructor Han 韓: The Commentary on the Judgments (Tuanzhuan) is clear, plain, and easy; originally there was nothing difficult to compose in it [?], yet the candidates instead all plagiarize hackneyed phrases, making them tiresome to read. This essay washes away the old to create the new; its reasoning is clear and its diction vigorous, bringing out the sage's intention in transmitting the hexagram Increase. It deserves to be placed among the superior selections.

彖傳釋卦名而廣益之義釋卦辭而申益之道
尤極言賛益之大也夫益非可以一言盡也彖

皇畫益之卦文王係益之辭吾夫子作彖傳以
釋之盖謂卦之所以名益者以卦體損上卦初
===
畫之陽益下卦初畫之陰是在上損己以益民
則其民感悅無窮盖若天澤之下注而悅物也
陽自上卦而下於下卦之下是自上降己以下
賢則其道顯著無外盖若天道之下濟而光明
也此皆釋卦名而廣益之義者若夫卦辭所謂
利有攸往者以卦體九五居中得正為君六二
居中得正為臣君臣具中正之道以益天下有
福被於民矣往何不利哉所謂利涉大川者以
卦象震位東方属木巽於易象為木二木為舟

Only in this essay does one see an exposition that is balanced, sound, and fluent.

The "Commentary on the Judgments" (Tuanzhuan 彖傳) explains the name of the hexagram and broadens the meaning of Increase (Yi 益); it explains the words of the hexagram and sets forth the Way of Increase; and it especially speaks to the utmost in praising the greatness of Increase. Now, Increase cannot be exhausted in a single word. When the "Commentary on the Judgments" broadens its meaning, sets forth its Way, and praises its greatness, has it not exhausted it completely? In antiquity, the August Fuxi (犧皇) drew the hexagram of Increase, King Wen (文王) appended the words of Increase, and our Master [Confucius] composed the "Commentary on the Judgments" to explain them. He meant that the reason the hexagram is named "Increase" is that, in the structure of the hexagram, the yang of the first line of the upper trigram is diminished to increase the yin of the first line of the lower trigram. This represents those above diminishing themselves to benefit the people, so that the people are moved to boundless joy—just like heavenly grace pouring down to gladden all things. And the yang coming from the upper trigram down below the lower trigram represents those above humbling themselves to condescend to the worthy, so that their Way becomes manifest everywhere without limit—just like the Way of Heaven descending to give aid and shining brightly. All of this explains the name of the hexagram and broadens the meaning of Increase. As for what the words of the hexagram call "favorable to have somewhere to go," it is because in the structure of the hexagram, the Nine in the Fifth place occupies the center and attains correctness as the ruler, while the Six in the Second place occupies the center and attains correctness as the minister. When ruler and minister possess the Way of centrality and correctness with which to benefit the world, blessings are bestowed upon the people—in going forward, what could be unfavorable? As for what is called "favorable for crossing the great river," it is because in the imagery of the hexagram, Zhen (震) is positioned in the east and belongs to wood, while Xun (巽) in the images of the Changes is also wood; the two woods form the [benefit of] boats…

title: 成化七年應天府鄉試錄
text:
楫之利以濟不通其道行於世矣涉何不利哉
此皆釋卦辭而申益之道者又卦德震以陽起
而德為動也巽以陰伏而德為巽也是人之益
道動而巽其日進廣大何有疆限哉卦體乾以
陽下施而成震也坤以陰上生而成巽也是天
地之道施而生其益物溥博何有方所哉是知
凡益之道皆視當益之時時未至也不先之時
既至也不後之惟與時而偕行耳此又極言賛
益之大者聖人彖傳之意可謂無餘蘊矣攷之
===
損益二卦義相對而序相承者彖傳於損則曰
損益盈虛與時偕行於益則曰凡益之道與時
偕行盖當損而損當益而益各有其時時者其
損益之準也然豈特是哉六十四卦三百八十
四爻舉不越乎時也孟子曰孔子聖之時然則
傳易之聖人其即易乎
易與天地準故能彌綸天地之道仰以觀
於天文俯以察於地理是故知幽明之
故

釋之利以濟不通其道行於世矣渉何不利哉
此皆釋卦辭而申益之道者又卦德震以陽起

道動而巽其日進廣大何有疆限哉卦體乾以

既至也不後之惟與時而偕行耳此又極言賛
益之大者聖人彖傳之意可謂無餘蘊矣攷之
===

損益盈虛與時偕行於益則曰凡益之道與時
偕行蓋當損而損當益而益各有其時時者其
損益之準也然豈特是哉六十四卦三百八十
四爻舉不越乎時也孟子曰孔子聖之時然則

易與天地準故能彌綸天地之道仰以觀
於天文俯以察於地理是故知幽明之
故
punctuated:
楫之利，以濟不通，其道行於世矣，涉何不利哉？此皆釋卦辭而申益之道者。又卦德，震以陽起而德為動也，巽以陰伏而德為巽也；是人之益道動而巽，其日進廣大何有疆限哉？卦體，乾以陽下施而成震也，坤以陰上生而成巽也；是天地之道施而生，其益物溥博何有方所哉？是知凡益之道，皆視當益之時。時未至也，不先之；時既至也，不後之，惟與時而偕行耳。此又極言賛益之大者，聖人《彖傳》之意，可謂無餘蘊矣。攷之損、益二卦，義相對而序相承者，《彖傳》於損則曰「損益盈虛，與時偕行」，於益則曰「凡益之道，與時偕行」。盖當損而損，當益而益，各有其時，時者，其損益之準也。然豈特是哉？六十四卦、三百八十四爻，舉不越乎時也。孟子曰：「孔子，聖之時。」然則傳《易》之聖人，其即《易》乎！
「《易》與天地準，故能彌綸天地之道。仰以觀於天文，俯以察於地理，是故知幽明之故。」
translation_en:
…and oars, by which one crosses where passage is blocked, so that the Way prevails in the world; how then could crossing not be advantageous? All these explain the hexagram statement and elaborate upon the Way of Increase (Yi 益). Furthermore, as for the virtues of the trigrams, Zhen 震 arises with yang and its virtue is movement, while Xun 巽 lies hidden with yin and its virtue is compliance; thus, in the human Way of Increase, moving with compliance, how could its daily advance in breadth and greatness have any boundary? As for the form of the hexagram, Qian 乾 bestows yang downward to form Zhen, and Kun 坤 generates yin upward to form Xun; thus, in the Way of Heaven and Earth, bestowing and generating, how could its vast benefit to things be confined to any single place? From this we know that all the Ways of Increase look to the proper time for increase. When the time has not yet arrived, one does not anticipate it; when the time has arrived, one does not lag behind it, but simply proceeds together with the time. This again speaks to the utmost in praising the greatness of Increase, and the meaning of the sage's Commentary on the Judgments (Tuanzhuan 彖傳) may be said to leave nothing unexpressed. Examining the two hexagrams Decrease (Sun 損) and Increase (Yi 益), whose meanings are opposite and whose sequence is continuous, the Commentary on the Judgments says under Decrease, "Decrease and increase, fullness and emptiness, proceed with the time," and under Increase it says, "All the Way of Increase proceeds with the time." Indeed, decreasing when one ought to decrease and increasing when one ought to increase each has its proper time; time is the standard for decrease and increase. Yet how could it be only this? None of the sixty-four hexagrams and three hundred and eighty-four lines goes beyond timing. Mencius (Mengzi 孟子) said: "Confucius (Kongzi 孔子) was the timely sage." If so, then was not the sage who transmitted the Changes (Yi 易) himself the Changes?

"The Changes are on a par with Heaven and Earth, and therefore can comprehensively weave together and order the Way of Heaven and Earth. Looking up, one contemplates the patterns of Heaven; looking down, one examines the configurations of Earth; therefore one knows the causes of darkness and light."

text:
蔣廷貴
同考試官教授韓批此題有定説而作者紛紛舛錯殊
無定見唯此篇説彌綸天地之道極為明白詳盡盖嘗潜
心於易者是用録出以示来學
同考試官監丞閻批此題首二句實一章綱領與下
文三節相應而天地之道本義已明言矣學者率不究心
故作此義者陳腐相襲首尾衡决殊無照應唯此篇深
合本義之旨且辭理煥然讀之令人心開神聳高薦何疑
考試官侍講徐批易道之大聖人用之此作發揮
===
盡矣其深於易者乎
考試官洗馬楊批此題多程文矣見是篇洗舊
説故録之
易道之大聖人用之窮乎理焉夫易準天地而
彌綸天地之道則易道可謂大矣聖人用之豈
不窮乎理哉何則易之為書也卦爻既立而理
道咸具是故天地大矣而卦也具有天地之道
而與之齊爻也亦具有天地之道而與之準惟
易準天地也故能彌綸天地之道焉彌如彌縫

translation_en:
Jiang Tinggui 蔣廷貴

Associate Examiner Instructor Han comments: There is an established explanation for this topic, yet examinees writing on it were confused and mistaken, completely lacking any settled view. Only this essay explains "encompassing and ordering the Way of Heaven and Earth" with extreme clarity and thoroughness, showing that the author has deeply immersed his mind in the Book of Changes (Yi). Therefore it is recorded and published here as a guide for future students.

Associate Examiner Directorate Proctor Yan comments: The first two sentences of this passage are truly the guiding thread of the entire chapter, corresponding to the three sections that follow below, and what is meant by "the Way of Heaven and Earth" has already been clearly stated in the Original Meaning of the Zhou Changes (Benyi). Scholars generally fail to apply their minds to this, so those who write expositions on this passage repeat stale clichés, with beginning and end disconnected and utterly lacking coherence. Only this essay accords deeply with the purport of the Original Meaning, and its diction and reasoning are brilliant; reading it opens the mind and uplifts the spirit. What doubt could there be in recommending him for a high rank!

Examiner Expositor-in-waiting Xu comments: The greatness of the Way of the Changes and how the sage puts it to use are fully brought out in this composition. Surely he is one who is profound in the Changes!

Examiner Librarian Yang comments: There have already been many model answers on this topic, but seeing that this essay washes away stale explanations, we have recorded it.

Because of the greatness of the Way of the Changes, the sage uses it to exhaustively fathom principle. Now, since the Changes is on a par with Heaven and Earth and encompasses and orders the Way of Heaven and Earth, the Way of the Changes may truly be called great; when the sage uses it, does he not exhaustively fathom principle? How so? As a book, once the hexagrams and lines of the Changes are established, principles and the Way are all complete within it. Therefore, great as Heaven and Earth are, the hexagrams possess the Way of Heaven and Earth and are equal to them, and the lines likewise possess the Way of Heaven and Earth and are on a par with them. Precisely because the Changes is on a par with Heaven and Earth, it is able to encompass and order the Way of Heaven and Earth. "Encompassing" (mi 彌) is like the mi in "stitching and sealing together" (mifeng 彌縫)…

title: 成化七年應天府鄉試錄
text:
之彌蓋卦爻於天地之道若幽明死生鬼神之
變知仁萬物晝夜之理皆併包揔括渾然無所
遺漏若彌縫之終竟聯合而無罅是能彌也綸
如絡絲之綸蓋卦爻彌縫之内若幽明死生鬼
神之殊知仁萬物晝夜之辨皆條分縷析粲然
不可殽亂若絡絲之選擇條理而無纇是能綸
也準天地而彌綸天地之道此易道之大矣聖
人用之何如耶蓋晝夜上下者天之文也天之
文在上且易見故聖人仰而以易觀焉南北高
===
深者地之理也地之理在下且難知故聖人俯
而以易察焉仰觀天文則晝明而夜幽上明而
下幽知天文幽明之所以然矣俯察地理則南
明而北幽高明而深幽知地理幽明之所以然
矣此聖人窮理之一端而窮理亦聖人用易之
一事耳暨乎盡其性至於命則聖人用易之事
盡而易道之大益可見矣抑考說卦有曰窮理
盡性以至於命而此言仰觀俯察以知幽明乃
窮理之事下文言知周萬物道濟天下則盡性

===
深者地之理也地之理在下且難知〔故〕〔聖〕聖人俯
而以易察焉仰觀天文則晝明而夜幽上明而
下幽知天文幽明之所以然矣俯察地理則南
明而北幽高明而深幽知地理幽明之所以然
矣此聖人窮理之一端而窮理亦聖人用易之
一事耳曁乎盡其性至於命則聖人用易之事
盡而易道之大益可見矣抑考說卦有曰窮理
盡性以至於命而此言仰觀俯察以知幽明乃
窮理之事下文言知周萬物道濟天下則盡性
punctuated: 之彌，蓋卦爻於天地之道，若幽明、死生、鬼神之變，知仁、萬物、晝夜之理，皆併包揔括，渾然無所遺漏，若彌縫之終竟聯合而無罅，是能彌也。綸如絡絲之綸，蓋卦爻彌縫之内，若幽明、死生、鬼神之殊，知仁、萬物、晝夜之辨，皆條分縷析，粲然不可殽亂，若絡絲之選擇條理而無纇，是能綸也。準天地而彌綸天地之道，此易道之大矣。聖人用之何如耶？蓋晝夜、上下者，天之文也；天之文在上且易見，故聖人仰而以《易》觀焉。南北、高深者，地之理也；地之理在下且難知，故聖人俯而以《易》察焉。仰觀天文，則晝明而夜幽，上明而下幽，知天文幽明之所以然矣；俯察地理，則南明而北幽，高明而深幽，知地理幽明之所以然矣。此聖人窮理之一端，而窮理亦聖人用《易》之一事耳。暨乎盡其性、至於命，則聖人用《易》之事盡，而《易》道之大益可見矣。抑考《說卦》有曰：「窮理盡性，以至於命。」而此言仰觀俯察以知幽明，乃窮理之事；下文言知周萬物、道濟天下，則盡性
translation_en:
…of “stitching up” (mifeng). For in regard to the Way of Heaven and Earth—such as the transformations of the obscure and the manifest, of life and death, and of ghosts and spirits, as well as the principles of wisdom and benevolence, of the myriad things, and of day and night—the hexagrams and lines encompass and summarize them all as an undifferentiated whole without omitting anything. Just as in stitching up, where everything is thoroughly joined together without a gap, so is it able to “encompass” (mi). “To order” (lun) is like the “reeling” in reeling silk. For within what the hexagrams and lines stitch together, the differences among the obscure and the manifest, life and death, and ghosts and spirits, as well as the distinctions among wisdom and benevolence, the myriad things, and day and night, are all divided into their threads and analyzed strand by strand, dazzlingly clear and impossible to confuse. Just as in reeling silk, where the threads are sorted and arranged in order without a knot, so is it able to “order” (lun). Being on a par with Heaven and Earth, and encompassing and ordering the Way of Heaven and Earth—such is the greatness of the Way of the Changes!

How, then, does the sage make use of it? Now, day and night, and above and below, are the patterns of Heaven. Because the patterns of Heaven are above and easy to see, the sage looks up and observes them by means of the Changes. South and north, and height and depth, are the principles of Earth. Because the principles of Earth are below and difficult to know, the sage looks down and examines them by means of the Changes. Looking up to observe the patterns of Heaven, one sees that day is manifest and night is obscure, that what is above is manifest and what is below is obscure, and thus knows the reason why the obscure and the manifest in the patterns of Heaven are so. Looking down to examine the principles of Earth, one sees that the south is manifest and the north is obscure, that the high is manifest and the deep is obscure, and thus knows the reason why the obscure and the manifest in the principles of Earth are so. This is one aspect of the sage’s exhausting of principle, and exhausting principle is likewise only one matter in the sage’s use of the Changes. When it comes to fulfilling his nature and arriving at Heaven’s decree, the work of the sage’s use of the Changes is complete, and the greatness of the Way of the Changes can be seen all the more.

Moreover, if we examine the Discussion of the Trigrams (Shuogua), it says: “They exhausted principle and fulfilled their nature, so as to arrive at Heaven’s decree.” What is said here about looking up to observe and looking down to examine in order to know the obscure and the manifest is the business of exhausting principle; what the text below says about wisdom encompassing the myriad things and the Way bringing aid to all under Heaven is the business of fulfilling nature…

translation_en:
…is the matter of [fully developing one's nature]; and when it further says, "compassing and molding heaven and earth, and intricately completing the myriad things," that is the matter of reaching the decree of Heaven. It is simply that the former passage speaks in terms of the Sages' creation of the Book of Changes (Yi), whereas this passage speaks in terms of the Sages' use of the Book of Changes. This being so, both those who created the Changes and those who used the Changes investigated principles to the utmost, fully developed their nature, and reached the decree of Heaven. "The former sages and the latter sages—their principles are one." How could these words deceive me!

Expositions on the Book of Documents (Shu yi)
"To calculate and delineate the movements and appearances of the sun, the moon, the stars, and the zodiacal spaces" (Li xiang ri yue xing chen).
By Bu Tong 卜同.
Associate Examiner and Instructor (jiaoyu) Li 李 comments: This essay explains the principles clearly and is written fluently; it captures Emperor Yao's intention in commissioning his officials.
Associate Examiner and Professor (jiaoshou) Fang 方 comments: This passage concerns the matter of reverently according with August Heaven. Although many candidates understand this, an essay that elucidates it so thoroughly and whose diction is as refined and succinct as this one is rarely found; it ought to be selected for publication.
Examiner and Expositor-in-waiting (shijiang) Xu 徐 comments: Able to portray the reality of Emperor Yao's reverent compliance with Heaven.
Examiner and Librarian (xima) Yang 楊 comments: This essay stands out uniquely from all the other compositions.

Using the Heaven that lies within human hands to match the Heaven that is in the sky—this is how the sage ruler, in commissioning his officials, reverently accorded with Heaven. For calendrical calculations and astronomical instruments (li xiang) represent the Heaven within human hands, whereas the sun, the moon, the stars, and the zodiacal spaces (ri yue xing chen) are the Heaven in the sky. When the sage ruler commissioned his officials to use the Heaven within human hands to match the Heaven in the sky, how was this anything other than a desire to fulfill the reality of reverently according with Heaven? In antiquity, Emperor Yao's thought was as if to say: In the Way of the ruler…

title: 成化七年應天府鄉試錄
text:
道莫重於敬順乎天所以敬順乎天莫先於曆
象曆所以紀數之書非曆無以紀天之數象所
以觀天之器非象無以觀天之象汝羲和可不
造曆制象乎夫日月星辰繫于天日月星辰之
數天之數也造乎曆則日月之遲速星辰之順
逆皆於是乎可考日月星辰懸于天日月星辰
之象天之象也制乎象則日月之運行星辰之
次舍皆於是乎可審以曆所紀之數與在天之
日月星辰而無差焉則一展手也可以得其遲
===
速順逆之詳不必推測於茫昧之際以象所觀
之象與在天之日月星辰而脗合焉則一舉目
也可以得其運行次舍之悉不必審察於輕清
之表以在人之天而合在天之天非所以敬順
天乎能如是則汝羲和之職亦於是乎盡矣抑
論帝堯之敬天無非欲造曆以勤民也故下文
曰敬授人時造曆之前以敬乎天是先天而天
弗違造曆之後以勤乎民是後天而奉天時聖
君於事何往非敬而况於敬天治民之大者乎

曰敬授人時造曆之前以敬乎天是先天而天
弗違造曆之後以勤乎民是後天而奉天時聖
君於事何往非敬而况於敬天治民之大者乎
punctuated:
道莫重於敬順乎天，所以敬順乎天莫先於曆象。曆，所以紀數之書，非曆無以紀天之數；象，所以觀天之器，非象無以觀天之象。汝羲、和可不造曆制象乎？夫日月星辰繫于天，日月星辰之數，天之數也，造乎曆，則日月之遲速、星辰之順逆，皆於是乎可考。日月星辰懸于天，日月星辰之象，天之象也，制乎象，則日月之運行、星辰之次舍，皆於是乎可審。以曆所紀之數，與在天之日月星辰而無差焉，則一展手也，可以得其遲速順逆之詳，不必推測於茫昧之際；以象所觀之象，與在天之日月星辰而脗合焉，則一舉目也，可以得其運行次舍之悉，不必審察於輕清之表。以在人之天，而合在天之天，非所以敬順天乎？能如是，則汝羲、和之職亦於是乎盡矣。」

抑論帝堯之敬天，無非欲造曆以勤民也。故下文曰「敬授人時」。造曆之前以敬乎天，是先天而天弗違；造曆之後以勤乎民，是後天而奉天時。聖君於事何往非敬，而况於敬天治民之大者乎？
translation_en:
…the Way [of a ruler], nothing is more important than reverently according with Heaven, and in the means of reverently according with Heaven, nothing takes precedence over calendrical calculations and astronomical instruments. The calendar is a book used to record numbers; without a calendar, there is no way to record the numbers of Heaven. The astronomical instrument is an apparatus used to observe Heaven; without an astronomical instrument, there is no way to observe the phenomena of Heaven. How could you, Xi and He, not compile a calendar and construct astronomical instruments? Now, the sun, moon, and stars are attached to Heaven; the numbers of the sun, moon, and stars are the numbers of Heaven. By compiling a calendar, the slowness and swiftness of the sun and moon, and the progressive and retrograde motions of the stars and celestial lodges, can all be verified therein. The sun, moon, and stars are suspended in Heaven; the phenomena of the sun, moon, and stars are the phenomena of Heaven. By constructing astronomical instruments, the revolutions of the sun and moon, and the stations and lodges of the stars, can all be examined therein. When the numbers recorded by the calendar have no discrepancy with the sun, moon, and stars in Heaven, then with a single stretch of the hand one can obtain the details of their slowness, swiftness, progression, and retrogradation, without needing to conjecture amidst vague obscurity. When the phenomena observed by the instrument match seamlessly with the sun, moon, and stars in Heaven, then with a single lift of the eyes one can obtain the full particulars of their revolutions, stations, and lodges, without needing to peer beyond the light and pure ether. To match the Heaven that is in Heaven by means of the Heaven that is in man—is this not the way to reverently accord with Heaven? If you can do this, then the duties of you, Xi and He, will also be fulfilled therein."

Furthermore, if we consider Emperor Yao's reverence for Heaven, it was nothing other than desiring to compile a calendar in order to be diligent on behalf of the people. Therefore, the text below says, "reverently grant the seasons to the people." Before compiling the calendar, he reveres Heaven: this is preceding Heaven, and Heaven does not act in opposition to him. After compiling the calendar, he is diligent on behalf of the people: this is following Heaven and respecting the timing of Heaven. In all affairs, where does a sage ruler not exercise reverence—and how much more so in the great matters of revering Heaven and governing the people?…

text:
吁帝堯之急先務於此亦可見矣
天壽平格保乂有殷
王献

字直以爲眷壽六臣令人厭觀此作能敷衍傳註爲

下文有殷嗣天滅威天曽不以壽之說證之無疑矣

大臣之留同列既論上天壽人之無私必舉前
臣壽國之有實夫天無私壽惟平格者則壽之
商之諸臣能盡平格之實豈不有以壽其國也
哉周公以是勉留召公意有在矣公意若曰天
人之際感應甚速天以至平爲心豈有私壽於
人哉惟人之至平通格于天者而後壽之焉善
者福之一天道之自然爾天以無私爲心豈有

大臣之留同列，既論上天壽人之無私，必舉前臣壽國之有實。夫天無私壽，惟平格者則壽之。商之諸臣能盡平格之實，豈不有以壽其國也哉？周公以是勉留召公，意有在矣。公意若曰：天人之際，感應甚速。天以至平爲心，豈有私壽於人哉？惟人之至平通格于天者，而後壽之焉。善者福之，一天道之自然爾。天以無私爲心，豈有
translation_en:
Alas! Emperor Yao's urgency regarding the foremost priorities can also be seen in this.

"Heaven gives longevity to the just and the intelligent; so those ministers maintained and regulated the empire of Yin."
Wang Xian
Comment by Associate Examiner Instructor Li: In the examination hall, many were stumped by this topic, taking the words "Heaven gives longevity" straightaway to mean favoring the six ministers with long life, which made them tiresome to read. This composition is able to elaborate on the commentaries to form its essay, and deserves to be selected.
Comment by Associate Examiner Instructor Fang: Those writing on this topic mostly expounded the characters ping [just] and ge [intelligent/reaching] separately, greatly missing the purport of the Classic. This essay neither misses the purport nor lacks a concise and antique style; he must be a scholar of learning.
Comment by Examiner Expositor-in-waiting Xu: This essay takes "maintained and regulated the empire of Yin" as giving longevity to the state. Verified against the explanation in the following passage—"the last successor of Yin was overwhelmed with steps of ruin by Heaven; did Heaven cease to give longevity?"—this is beyond doubt.
Comment by Examiner Librarian Yang: A short essay on the Documents [?; 短夏, likely for 短書 or 短篇] values richness and fullness; this composition achieves it.

When a great minister retains his colleague in office, having argued that High Heaven has no partiality in granting longevity to men, he must cite the concrete reality of former ministers granting longevity to the state. Now, Heaven does not grant longevity out of partiality; only to those who are evenly just and reach through to Heaven [pingge] does it grant longevity. Since the various ministers of Shang were able to fulfill the reality of being evenly just and reaching Heaven, how could they not thereby grant longevity to their state? When the Duke of Zhou used this to encourage the Duke of Shao to remain, his intention lay herein. The Duke's meaning was as if to say: Between Heaven and man, stimulus and response are extremely swift. Heaven takes utmost fairness as its mind; how could it partially grant longevity to anyone? Only when a person's utmost fairness reaches through to Heaven does it thereafter grant longevity to him. Bringing good fortune to the good is simply the natural course of the Way of Heaven. Heaven takes impartiality as its mind; how could it…

title: 成化七年應天府鄉試錄
text:
於人而私壽之哉惟人之無私通徹于天者而
後壽之焉栽者培之一天理之當然爾是豈無
徵之言哉觀諸有商六臣可見矣若伊尹佐成
湯以聖輔聖其治化格于皇天伊陟臣扈佐大
戊以賢輔賢其治化格于上帝以至巫咸巫賢
甘盤之為佐莫非能盡平格之實故能保孚休
之治于有殷多歷年所而眷命之無疆非天壽
之而何保嘉靖之治于有商惟有歷年而申命
之無巳又非天壽之而何是殷得天之壽由乎
===
六臣之所致六臣心在王室惟欲殷壽豈計其
私哉殷之六臣壽國之實若此今汝召公曾不
以此為念以圖匹休何汲汲以求去哉抑觀周
公之留召公首言憂國之心非人所知次言天
民可畏惟人是賴又次言殷先王與文武得人
之助然文王時五人至武王時四人今惟我二

Only when a man's impartiality penetrates through to Heaven does Heaven grant him longevity; that it nurtures that which is upright is simply the natural principle of Heaven. How could these be unsubstantiated words? One can see it by looking at the six ministers of the Shang: for instance, Yi Yin assisted Cheng Tang, a sage aiding a sage, and their transformative governance reached Sovereign Heaven; Yi Zhi and Chen Hu assisted Tai Wu, worthies aiding a worthy, and their transformative governance reached the Lord on High; and down to Wu Xian, Wu Xian, and Gan Pan serving as assistants, there were none who did not fulfill the reality of being just and reaching Heaven. Therefore, they were able to preserve a trustworthy and blessed rule in Yin through the passage of many years, with Heaven's favoring mandate boundless—what was this if not Heaven granting it longevity? And they preserved a fine and tranquil rule in Shang through the passage of years, with its renewed mandate unceasing—what was this, too, if not Heaven granting it longevity? Thus, that Yin obtained longevity from Heaven was brought about by the six ministers. The hearts of the six ministers were with the royal house; desiring only the longevity of Yin, how could they calculate their own private interests? Such was the reality of how the six ministers of Yin gave longevity to the state; yet now you, the Duke of Shao, do not even take this to heart so as to plan to match their glory—why are you so anxious to seek departure? Moreover, looking at how the Duke of Zhou urged the Duke of Shao to stay: first he said that his heart, anxious for the state, was not understood by others; next he said that Heaven and the people are to be stood in awe of, and that everything depends upon capable men; and next again he spoke of how the former kings of Yin and Kings Wen and Wu obtained the assistance of capable men. Yet in King Wen's time there were five men, by King Wu's time there were four, and now there are only the two of us. If you, sir, seek to leave out of concern over fullness of success and high station, how could I alone be able to bear the burden? Indeed, because his anxiety was deep, his plea to stay was earnest; and because his plea to stay was earnest, his words were detailed. Sharing the same merit and forming a single body with him, and equally possessing a heart loyal to the ruler and devoted to the state, how could the Duke of Shao not be moved…

福頌禱之無已其情不亦至乎是詩諸侯所必
荅桑扈也盖感天子之德而極頌禱之情故托
物以起興曰鴛鴦于飛則畢之羅之矣
吾願君子萬年則福禄自宜之焉繼而興曰鴛

則宜其享遐福焉夫萬年則黃髮兒齒而壽考
無疆矣福禄謂之宜則福禄享之而適當所謂
俾爾戬穀罄無不宜者矣福謂之遐則福禄宜
之而久遠所謂降爾遐福惟日不足者矣壽既

translation_en: …and blessings in his prayers of praise without cease—is not his sentiment indeed at its utmost? This ode is that with which the feudal lords responded [必 for 以?] to the "Sanghu" ("Blue-green Finches"). For being moved by the virtue of the Son of Heaven, they carried their sentiments of praise and prayer to the utmost. Therefore the poet draws upon an object to initiate an evocative image (xing), saying: "When the mandarin ducks are in flight, one catches them with hand-nets and spread-nets; I wish that the lord may live for ten thousand years, and that felicity and emolument may naturally befit him." Continuing, he raises the image, saying: "When the mandarin ducks are on the fish-dam, they tuck in their left wings to roost side by side; I wish that the lord may live for ten thousand years, and that it may befit him to enjoy far-reaching felicity." Now, "ten thousand years" means having yellow hair and childlike teeth, a longevity without bound. When felicity and emolument are said to "befit" him, it means he enjoys felicity and emolument in due measure, as in the saying, "May He grant you all excellence, so that there is nothing not befitting." When felicity is called "far-reaching," it means that felicity and emolument befit him enduringly, as in the saying, "He sends down to you far-reaching felicity, for which the very days seem insufficient." With longevity already at ten thousand years, and felicity and emolument befitting him, and that felicity moreover far-reaching and enduring—to praise and pray for him thus would seem to have reached the utmost, and yet his sentiment is still not satisfied. Thus he again draws upon another object to initiate an evocative image, saying that "when the team of four horses is in the stable, one not only feeds them with chopped hay, but also grains them with millet; I wish that the lord may live for ten thousand years, and that felicity and emolument may nourish him." Continuing, he again says that "when the team of four horses is in the stable, one not only grains them with millet, but also feeds them with chopped hay; I wish that the lord may live for ten thousand years, and that felicity and emolument may give him repose." Now, the utmost longevity cannot exceed ten thousand years, so he repeats it time and again without changing the words. When felicity and emolument are said to "nourish" (ai), it means that felicity and emolument nurture him like the fostering of rivers and seas, never exhausted; when they are said to "give repose" (sui), it means that felicity and emolument secure him like the firmness of ridges and hills, never altering. "To nourish" goes beyond merely "befitting," and "to give repose" goes…

止於艾，頌禱之詞，於是乎至矣。吁！鴛鴦也，乗馬也，屢託之以起興；萬年也，福禄也，屢頌之而不已。盖臣之於君，不敢擬議其德，而惟極頌禱之情，敬之至也；頌禱而極言其壽福之無已，愛之至也。非周之諸侯，孰能爾耶？抑觀上篇，天子燕諸侯，則極言其德之盛；此篇諸侯荅天子，則極頌其福之隆。上之美下以德者，愛其下也；下之頌上以福者，忠其上也。上下交而德業成矣。有周享八百年之盛，有以夫！

translation_en:
… stop at "nourishing"; with this, the words of praise and prayer reach their utmost! Ah! Mandarin ducks and teams of horses are repeatedly invoked as evocative metaphors; ten thousand years, felicity, and emolument are repeatedly extolled without ceasing. For in the relation of a minister to his ruler, he does not presume to evaluate or debate his virtue, but solely exhausts the feelings of praise and prayer—this is the utmost of reverence. In praising and praying, to speak to the fullest of his boundless longevity and felicity—this is the utmost of affection. Who but the feudal lords of Zhou could be capable of this? Moreover, looking at the preceding ode, when the Son of Heaven feasts the feudal lords, he speaks to the fullest of the abundance of their virtue; in this ode, when the feudal lords reply to the Son of Heaven, they extol to the fullest the magnificence of his felicity. That the superior praises his inferiors for their virtue is because he loves his inferiors; that the inferiors extol their superior with wishes for felicity is because they are loyal to their superior. When superior and inferior are in communion, virtuous enterprise is achieved. That the house of Zhou enjoyed eight hundred years of prosperity was indeed for good reason!

"The capital of Shang is well-ordered, the standard of the four quarters." (Book of Odes, Shang song, "Yinwu")
Wu Hui 吳徽
Associate Examiner, Instructor Zheng 鄭 comments: Among the more than nine hundred scripts on the Book of Odes (Shijing) in this ward, those who wrote on this topic were florid, heterogeneous, and contrary to its fundamental purport. Only this essay is pure, refined, and classically elegant; the spirit of the people of Shang singing in praise of the restoration under Gaozong 高宗 is vividly visible. He must be one who has applied his mind to fundamental principles.
Associate Examiner, Instructor Zheng 鄭 comments: Most writers framed their arguments around the founding of the capital, which entirely misses the fundamental purport. Only this essay grasps the intention of the poet, depicting the spirit of restoration—admirable, truly admirable!
Examiner, Expositor-in-waiting Xu 徐 comments: This composition alone is able to capture and describe the spirit of the restoration under Gaozong.

title: 成化七年應天府鄉試錄
text:
考試官洗馬楊批此卷七篇皆嘉商邑其尤也
惟王都之整敕為天下之儀表此高宗中興而
然也夫有商之都舊矣至於高宗而整敕焉豈
不足以為天下之儀表乎此詩舊說以為祀高
宗之樂也商自成湯都亳至盤庚改而殷道衰
王都之勢委靡陵夷人慢易之也久矣高宗出
焉上敬天命下畏民嵒其賞也不僭其罰也不
濫庶政振舉於邦畿千里之間百度脩明於景
山維河之域故商邑翼翼整敕而起人之敬畏
===
非若昔之委靡而人慢視之矣肅肅嚴正而動
人之瞻仰非若向之陵夷而人易視之矣由是
自西自東小大之國政教皆於是乎取法豈但
歲事来辟以祈不譴乎自南自北遠近之邦政
教皆於是乎取正豈但稼穡匪懈以兾不咎乎
是則商邑之翼翼良為四方之極矣高宗中興
之氣象如此宜乎詩人頌之以為奉祀之樂歌
也抑又攷之商高宗周宣王皆樹中興之業者
也然宣王之政衰於暮年故一傳而幽王大壞

考試官洗馬楊批：此卷七篇皆嘉，「商邑」其尤也。

惟王都之整敕，為天下之儀表，此高宗中興而然也。夫有商之都舊矣，至於高宗而整敕焉，豈不足以為天下之儀表乎？此《詩》舊說以為祀高宗之樂也。商自成湯都亳，至盤庚改而殷道衰，王都之勢委靡陵夷，人慢易之也久矣。高宗出焉，上敬天命，下畏民嵒，其賞也不僭，其罰也不濫，庶政振舉於邦畿千里之間，百度脩明於景山維河之域。故「商邑翼翼」，整敕而起人之敬畏，非若昔之委靡而人慢視之矣；肅肅嚴正而動人之瞻仰，非若向之陵夷而人易視之矣。由是自西自東，小大之國，政教皆於是乎取法，豈但歲事来辟以祈不譴乎？自南自北，遠近之邦，政教皆於是乎取正，豈但稼穡匪懈以兾不咎乎？是則「商邑之翼翼」，良為「四方之極」矣。高宗中興之氣象如此，宜乎詩人頌之，以為奉祀之樂歌也。抑又攷之，商高宗、周宣王皆樹中興之業者也。然宣王之政衰於暮年，故一傳而幽王大壞，
translation_en:
Comment by Examiner Yang, Librarian of the Left Secretariat of the Heir Apparent: All seven essays on this examination paper are admirable, and this one on "The city of Shang" is the finest among them.

That the orderliness of the royal capital served as a model for all under Heaven came about through the dynastic restoration of Gaozong. Now, the capital of the Shang had existed for a long time; when by the reign of Gaozong it was brought into order, how could it fail to serve as a model for all under Heaven? The old interpretation of this Ode holds that it was ceremonial music for sacrificing to Gaozong. Ever since Tang the Completer established the Shang capital at Bo, down to the time when Pan Geng changed the capital, the Way of Yin declined; the condition of the royal capital grew listless and dilapidated, and people had long treated it with disrespect and slight. Then Gaozong arose: above, he revered the Mandate of Heaven; below, he stood in awe of the rugged dangerousness of the common people. In his rewards he did not overstep; in his punishments he was not excessive. All the myriad affairs of administration were reinvigorated within the thousand li of the royal domain, and all the hundred institutions were cultivated and made bright within the territory bounded by Mount Jing and the Yellow River. Therefore, "the city of Shang was well-ordered" ("Shangyi yiyi")—disciplined and orderly, inspiring reverence and awe in people, no longer listless as in the past when people looked upon it with disrespect; solemn and strictly upright, stirring people to look up in admiration, no longer dilapidated as before when people looked upon it lightly. Consequently, from west and from east, states both small and great all took their model for governance and instruction from here—how could it merely be that they came to the ruler for seasonal affairs in hopes of escaping reprimand? From south and from north, lands both far and near all took their standard for governance and instruction from here—how could it merely be that they were unremitting in husbandry in hopes of avoiding blame? Thus "the well-ordered state of the city of Shang" truly served as "the standard for the four quarters" ("sifang zhi ji"). Such was the grand spirit of Gaozong's restoration; fitting indeed was it that the poet praised him, making this a musical song for offering sacrifices. Moreover, if we examine the matter further, both Gaozong of Shang and King Xuan of Zhou established the achievements of a dynastic restoration. Yet King Xuan's governance declined in his twilight years, so that after a single transmission of the throne, under King You everything was utterly ruined, …

translation_en:
… and the royal carriage of Zhou consequently moved east. Gaozong, on the other hand, heard the learning of the sages through Fu Yue, maintained a single-minded virtue from beginning to end, and brought peace and order to the state of Yin. Two generations later, moreover, there was Zu Jia, who protected and showed kindness to the common people and did not mistreat the widowed and solitary—something King Xuan could not match. Oh, how magnificent!

Exposition on the Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu)

"In spring, in the king's first month, the army halted at Lang to wait for the men of Chen and the men of Cai. On the jiawu day, the troops were drilled. In summer, our army and the army of Qi besieged Cheng; Cheng surrendered to the army of Qi. In autumn, the army returned." [All from the eighth year of Duke Zhuang.]

Zheng Da 鄭達

Comment by Associate Examiner Instructor (jiaoyu) Chen: [The topic is very clear, yet because of what the commentaries say, [candidates often mis?]understand it. Some base their argument on the weightiness of military action, not knowing that Master Hu's (Hu Anguo 胡安國) purport does not cover the drilling of troops; others base their argument on special historiography, not knowing that Master Chen's (Chen Fuliang 陳傅良) purport does not cover the besieging of Cheng. Only in this essay do we see both a true and thorough comprehension and concise, ancient phrasing.]
Comment by Examiner Expositor-in-Waiting (shijiang) Xu: [The style is mature and vigorous, not comparable to those who merely compose ordinary parallel clauses of four and six characters.]
Comment by Examiner Librarian (xima) Yang: [This is from a seasoned brush; it ought to be recorded for publication.]

The Spring and Autumn Annals records in detail the use of military force by a prestigious state in order to make manifest the extreme unrighteousness of that prestigious state. Regarding this campaign in the eighth year of Duke Zhuang of Lu—waging war without just cause and harming the people without achievement—the Spring and Autumn Annals writes it down in full in order to show censure. Now, military force is something the sages used only when they had no alternative. Why, then, did Duke Zhuang fail to abide by the counsels of the sages and remain ignorant of military discipline, going so far that in the spring of his eighth year, at the very beginning of the year…

title: 成化七年應天府鄉試錄
text:
之首親率三軍出駐于外盖以陳蔡將過而欲
邀之也躬提大衆次止于郎惟以陳蔡未至而
且俟之也既非折衝禦侮之舉又非除暴禁亂
之為是無名矣既而陳蔡不至師旅乆暴乃申
軍法以整飭之俾無失伍離次之患也嚴號令
以齊一之俾無逃亡潰散之虞也然既非大易
以律之師又非司馬四時之教是黷武矣遂夫
是年之夏又及齊以圍郕齊仇讐也廼比而親
之郕同姓也廼忍而伐之故郕忿魯之暴而甘
===
齊之降欵不納於曲阜之師俘不獻於東蒙之
廟不謂之無功可乎至於兹歲之秋爰下令以
班師歷三時矣始返斾而休幾一歲矣方解甲
而息則暴師已乆而勞民已甚戰鬭廢耕耘之
業供億空杼柚之貲不謂之害民可乎夫不惟
無名黷武而尤無功害民此莊公之師非義之
甚矣春秋詳而書之其為世戒也不亦深切著
明矣乎抑莊公之失盖不止此觀其乾時有戰
而納讐人之嗣如齊觀社而結讐人之婚雖曰

之首親率三軍出駐于外蓋以陳蔡將過而欲
邀之也躬提大衆次止于郎惟以陳蔡未至而
且俟之也既非折衝禦侮之舉又非除暴禁亂
之爲是無名矣既而陳蔡不至師旅久暴乃申

齊之降款不納於曲阜之師俘不獻於東蒙之
廟不謂之無功可乎至於茲歲之秋爰下令以
班師歷三時矣始返斾而休幾一歲矣方解甲
而息則暴師已久而勞民已甚戰鬬廢耕耘之
業供億空杼柚之貲不謂之害民可乎夫不惟
無名黷武而尤無功害民此莊公之師非義之
甚矣春秋詳而書之其爲世戒也不亦深切著
明矣乎抑莊公之失蓋不止此觀其乾時有戰
而納讐人之嗣如齊觀社而結讐人之婚雖曰
punctuated: 之首，親率三軍，出駐于外，盖以陳、蔡將過而欲邀之也；躬提大衆，次止于郎，惟以陳、蔡未至而且俟之也。既非折衝禦侮之舉，又非除暴禁亂之為，是無名矣。既而陳、蔡不至，師旅乆暴，乃申軍法以整飭之，俾無失伍離次之患也；嚴號令以齊一之，俾無逃亡潰散之虞也。然既非《大易》以律之師，又非司馬四時之教，是黷武矣。遂夫是年之夏，又及齊以圍郕。齊，仇讐也，廼比而親之；郕，同姓也，廼忍而伐之。故郕忿魯之暴而甘齊之降，欵不納於曲阜之師，俘不獻於東蒙之廟，不謂之無功可乎？至於兹歲之秋，爰下令以班師。歷三時矣，始返斾而休；幾一歲矣，方解甲而息。則暴師已乆而勞民已甚，戰鬭廢耕耘之業，供億空杼柚之貲，不謂之害民可乎？夫不惟無名、黷武，而尤無功、害民，此莊公之師非義之甚矣。《春秋》詳而書之，其為世戒也，不亦深切著明矣乎！抑莊公之失，盖不止此。觀其乾時有戰而納讐人之嗣，如齊觀社而結讐人之婚，雖曰…
translation_en:
…beginning of the year, personally led the three armies out to camp in the field, for Chen and Cai were about to pass by and he wished to intercept them; he personally led the great host and halted at Lang, solely because Chen and Cai had not yet arrived and he was waiting for them for the time being. Since this was neither an action to repel assault and ward off insult, nor an act to eliminate tyranny and suppress disorder, it was without just cause.

When presently Chen and Cai did not arrive and the troops had long been exposed in the field, he then reiterated military law to put them in order, so that there would be no trouble of losing ranks or leaving stations; and he made strict his commands to render them uniform, so that there would be no worry of desertion or scattering in rout. Yet since this was neither an army kept in discipline as in the Great Changes (Dayi), nor the seasonal training of the Minister of War (Sima), it was a wanton display of force.

Then, coming to the summer of that year [逮夫 rendered 遂夫], he further joined with Qi to besiege Cheng. Qi was a sworn enemy, yet he aligned with and drew close to it; Cheng was a state of the same surname, yet he had the heart to attack it. Therefore Cheng resented the brutality of Lu and willingly surrendered to Qi. Terms of submission were not received by the army of Qufu, and captives were not presented at the ancestral temple beneath Mount Dongmeng—can this not be called devoid of achievement?

Come the autumn of this year, he finally issued the order to withdraw the troops. Three seasons had passed before they first turned back their banners to rest; nearly a full year had elapsed before they at last unstrung their armor to repose. Thus the army had been exposed for a long time and the people exhausted to the extreme; fighting caused the work of plowing and weeding to be abandoned, and military provisioning emptied the wealth of shuttle and loom—can this not be called harming the people?

Now, not only was it without just cause and a wanton display of force, it was even more devoid of achievement and harmful to the people: this expedition of Duke Zhuang was the height of unrighteousness. When the Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu) records it in detail, is not the warning it provides to the world profound, incisive, and manifestly clear!

Moreover, Duke Zhuang's failings did not stop here. Observe how he fought the battle at Ganshi to install the heir of his enemy, and went to Qi to view the sacrifice at the altar of the soil in order to contract a marriage with his enemy; although one might say that…

復貶其僭此齊桓之伐戎獻捷嬰齊之會蜀盟
蜀春秋致謹於書法也且齊桓中國之伯主也
今因北戎病燕職貢不至遽提一國之師越千
里之險為燕闢地以伐戎人是不務德而勤兵
遠伐也春秋書人以譏其非矣既而以其所獲
躬示于魯蓋誇其得雋之績而耀其用武之威
punctuated:
以德報怨，於齊厚矣，然而忍心害理，於君父不亦薄乎？噫！魯以秉禮之國，而所行尚如此，吾於他何尤！

「齊人伐山戎」〔莊公三十年〕、「齊侯來獻戎捷」〔莊公〕〔三十一年〕、「公會楚公子嬰齊于蜀」、「公及楚人、秦人、宋人、陳人、衛人、鄭人、齊人、曹人、邾人、薛人、鄫人盟于蜀」〔並成公二年〕
吳邠

考試官侍講徐批：〔深得本傳之旨。〕
考試官洗馬楊批：〔辭達而已矣，此作庶乎。〕

《春秋》譏伯主伐遠而尤抑其誇，責外臣凌內而復貶其僭。此齊桓之伐戎、獻捷，嬰齊之會蜀、盟蜀，《春秋》致謹於書法也。且齊桓，中國之伯主也。今因北戎病燕，職貢不至，廼提一國之師，越千里之險，為燕闢地，以伐戎人，是不務德而勤兵遠伐也，《春秋》書「人」以譏其非矣。既而以其所獲躬示于魯，蓋誇其得雋之績，而耀其用武之威…
translation_en:
…returning good for injury, which was generous toward Qi indeed; yet in being callous of heart and violating moral principle, was he not all too ungenerous toward his ruler and father? Alas! If Lu, a state that upheld the rites, acted in such a way, how can we blame the others?

"A man of Qi attacked the Mountain Rong" [Thirtieth year of Duke Zhuang]; "The Marquis of Qi came to present the spoils of the Rong" [Thirty-first year of Duke Zhuang]; "The Duke met Prince Yingqi of Chu at Shu"; "The Duke made a covenant with men of Chu, Qin, Song, Chen, Wei, Zheng, Qi, Cao, Zhu, Xie, and Zeng at Shu" [Both in the second year of Duke Cheng].

By Wu Bin 吳邠.
Comment by Associate Examiner Instructor Chen: [Grounded in the commentaries and annotations, it expounds the historiography; this essay achieves that.]
Comment by Examiner Expositor-in-Waiting Xu: [Deeply grasps the purport of the commentary.]
Comment by Examiner Librarian Yang: ["In words, it is enough that they convey the meaning"—this composition comes close to that.]

The Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu) criticizes a hegemon for campaigning afar and especially curbs his boasting; it reproves an outer minister for encroaching upon the interior and further demotes him for his presumption. This is why, in Duke Huan of Qi's campaign against the Rong and presentation of spoils, and in Yingqi's meeting at Shu and covenant at Shu, the Spring and Autumn Annals exercised the utmost care in its historiographical phrasing. Now Duke Huan of Qi was the hegemon of the Central States. Because the Northern Rong were harassing Yan so that its tribute did not arrive, he led the army of an entire state across the hazards of a thousand li to open up territory for Yan by attacking the people of Rong. This was failing to cultivate virtue while mobilizing troops for a distant campaign; thus the Spring and Autumn Annals wrote "a man" to criticize his error. Soon afterward, he personally displayed what he had captured to Lu, seeking to boast of his achievement in winning a prize victory and to flaunt his martial might…

title: 成化七年應天府鄉試錄
text:
也殊不知諸侯不相遺俘可以方伯之貴而行
奉上之禮於鄰國乎春秋書曰來獻抑其誇也
前書人則疑微者故後書侯以見伐戎之人即
獻捷之侯耳若夫嬰齊者荆楚之大夫也今因
郤克戰鞌齊師撓敗廼假救齊之名為陽橋之
役因魯請平會公于蜀是脅衆威魯而以臣抗
君也春秋書名以著其實矣既而列卿匱盟詔
神于蜀盖乗其勝魯之勢而肆其駕晉之謀也
殊不知裔夷不當謀夏可以楚臣之賤而主禮
===
樂之權於中國乎降而稱人貶其僭也前稱名
氏則疑褒辭故後書人以見會蜀之公子即盟
蜀之人耳即是而觀齊桓之過楚人之罪昭昭
於筆削之間矣雖然齊桓之伐山戎固可貶矣
後日服楚召陵其不可予乎楚之公子主盟中
國固可責矣使中國力足以制之其有是乎此
齊伯之所以猶盛而晉伯之所以日衰也歟
禮記義
故天不愛其道地不愛其寶人不愛其情

樂之權於中國乎降而稱人貶其僭也前稱名

蜀之人耳即是而觀齊桓之過楚人之罪昭昭

禮記義
故天不愛其道地不愛其寶人不愛其情
punctuated:
也。殊不知諸侯不相遺俘，可以方伯之貴，而行奉上之禮於鄰國乎？《春秋》書曰「來獻」，抑其誇也。前書「人」，則疑微者；故後書「侯」，以見伐戎之人即獻捷之侯耳。若夫嬰齊者，荆楚之大夫也。今因郤克戰鞌，齊師撓敗，廼假救齊之名，為陽橋之役；因魯請平，會公于蜀，是脅衆威魯，而以臣抗君也。《春秋》書名，以著其實矣。既而列卿匱盟，詔神于蜀，盖乗其勝魯之勢，而肆其駕晉之謀也。殊不知裔夷不當謀夏，可以楚臣之賤，而主禮樂之權於中國乎？降而稱「人」，貶其僭也。前稱名氏，則疑褒辭；故後書「人」，以見會蜀之公子即盟蜀之人耳。即是而觀，齊桓之過、楚人之罪，昭昭於筆削之間矣。雖然，齊桓之伐山戎，固可貶矣，後日服楚召陵，其不可予乎？楚之公子主盟中國，固可責矣，使中國力足以制之，其有是乎？此齊伯之所以猶盛，而晉伯之所以日衰也歟！

禮記義
故天不愛其道，地不愛其寶，人不愛其情。
translation_en:
… Yet he utterly failed to realize that feudal lords do not present captives to one another; how could one of the noble rank of a regional hegemon perform a ritual meant for presenting spoils to a superior toward a neighboring state? The Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu) records this as "came to present [spoils]" in order to curb his boasting. Because the earlier entry recorded simply "a man [of Qi]," one might suspect it referred to a person of low rank; therefore, the later entry records "the Marquis [of Qi]" to show that the "man" who attacked the Rong was none other than the Marquis who presented the spoils of victory.

As for Yingqi, he was a Great Officer of Jing-Chu. At this time, because Xi Ke fought at An and the army of Qi was routed and defeated, Yingqi used the pretext of rescuing Qi to launch the campaign at Yangqiao. When Lu requested peace, he met the Duke at Shu; this was coercing the multitude to overawe Lu, and a minister standing as an equal against a ruler. The Spring and Autumn Annals records his personal name in order to make the reality of the matter manifest. Soon afterward, with the ranked ministers lacking aproper covenant, he called upon the spirits to witness the covenant at Shu; this was taking advantage of his momentum in prevailing over Lu to indulge his scheme of surpassing Jin. Yet he utterly failed to realize that frontier barbarians ought not to plot against the central Xia states; how could someone of the lowly status of a Chu minister preside over the authority of rites and music in the Central States? Demoting him and referring to him simply as "a man [of Chu]" was to censure his usurpation. Because the earlier entry referred to him by his clan title and personal name ("Prince Yingqi"), one might suspect it was an expression of praise; therefore, the later entry records "a man [of Chu]" to show that the Prince who met at Shu was none other than the "man" who covenanted at Shu.

Viewed in this light, the fault of Duke Huan of Qi and the offense of the man of Chu are made crystal clear through the recording and deleting of the sage's brush. Nevertheless, while Duke Huan of Qi's campaign against the Mountain Rong is certainly worthy of censure, in later days when he brought Chu to submission at Shaoling, can we not grant him approval? And while the Prince of Chu presiding over a covenant in the Central States is certainly worthy of reproach, had the strength of the Central States been sufficient to keep him in check, would such a thing have occurred? Is this not the reason why the hegemony of Qi was still flourishing, whereas the hegemony of Jin fell into daily decline?

Exposition on the Record of Rites (Liji)

"Therefore Heaven does not begrudge its Way, Earth does not begrudge its treasures, and Man does not begrudge his feelings." …

title: 成化七年應天府鄉試錄
text:
故天降膏露地出醴泉山出器車河出
馬圖鳳皇麒麟皆在郊棷龜龍在宮沼
其餘鳥獸之卵胎皆可俯而闚也則是
無故先王能脩禮以達義體信以達順
故此順之實也

說場中作者素虧講究不浮於辭則昧於理惟此卷

===
考試官侍講徐批先王大順之實此作能發之
考試官洗馬楊批發明大順之旨繁而不亂
作手也
觀天地人物之協應由先王盛德之感召此大
順之實也盖脩禮達義體信達順此先王之盛
德也盛德感召而天地人物無不協應焉豈非
大順之實哉記禮運者若謂先王大順之世三

故天降膏露，地出醴泉，山出器車，河出馬圖，鳳皇、麒麟皆在郊棷，龜、龍在宮沼，其餘鳥獸之卵胎，皆可俯而闚也。則是無故，先王能脩禮以達義，體信以達順，故此順之實也。
同考試官訓導羅批：此題天地人物同一大順，已有定說。場中作者素虧講究，不浮於辭則昧於理。惟此卷體認親切，辭簡理明，其必深於《禮》者，可羡，可羡！
考試官侍講徐批：先王大順之實，此作能發之。
考試官洗馬楊批：發明大順之旨，繁而不亂，作手也。
觀天地人物之協應，由先王盛德之感召，此大順之實也。盖脩禮達義、體信達順，此先王之盛德也；盛德感召，而天地人物無不協應焉，豈非大順之實哉？記《禮運》者若謂：先王大順之世，三才為之協應。是故道原於天，天不愛道，賦予盡其所有而不秘矣；寶興於地，地不愛寶，發育盡…
translation_en:
… Thus Heaven sends down sweet dew, Earth brings forth sweet springs, the mountains produce ceremonial vessels and carriages, the Yellow River brings forth the horse-chart, phoenixes and qilin are all in the suburban marshes, tortoises and dragons are in the palace ponds, and as for the eggs and offspring of the remaining birds and beasts, one can bend down and peer into their nests. Now this comes about for no other reason than that the former kings were able to cultivate ritual to carry out righteousness, and embody good faith to achieve harmony; thus this is the reality of harmony."

Comment by Associate Examiner and Assistant Instructor Luo: That Heaven, Earth, human beings, and things all share in one Great Harmony in this passage has an established interpretation. Candidates in the examination hall ordinarily lack thorough study of it, so if they are not superficial in their phrasing, they are muddled in their grasp of the principle. Only this paper grasps the meaning intimately, with concise language and clear reasoning. Its author must be someone deeply versed in the Record of Rites—truly admirable, truly admirable!

Comment by Examiner and Expositor-in-waiting Xu: This composition is able to bring out the reality of the former kings' Great Harmony.

Comment by Examiner and Librarian Yang: It elucidates the purport of Great Harmony, rich in detail yet free of disorder—the work of a skilled hand.

When we observe how the harmonious response of Heaven, Earth, human beings, and things stems from the inspiring call of the former kings' abundant virtue, we see that this is the reality of Great Harmony. For cultivating ritual to carry out righteousness and embodying good faith to achieve harmony constituted the abundant virtue of the former kings; when abundant virtue called them forth, Heaven, Earth, human beings, and things all responded in harmony—is this not the reality of Great Harmony? It is as if the recorder of the "Evolution of Rites" ("Liyun") were saying: In the age of the former kings' Great Harmony, the Three Powers responded in concert. Therefore, the Way originates in Heaven, and Heaven does not begrudge its Way, bestowing all that it possesses without keeping anything hidden; treasures arise from Earth, and Earth does not begrudge its treasures, generating and nurturing to the utmost…

title: 成化七年應天府鄉試錄
text:
其所有而不蓄矣情發於人人不愛其情盡所
有而發之矣故膏露降于天也其澤如膏之濃
而異乎常露醴泉出乎地也其味如醴之甘而
異乎常泉山出乎器車為希世之物河出乎馬
圖為文明之瑞鳳皇麒麟世不常有也今皆在
於郊內之棷靈龜神龍人不常見也今皆在於
宮中之沼其餘鳥之卵獸之胎皆可俯而闚而
無獝狘之患天地人物同一大順如此豈無故
而然哉由先王能脩此禮以為教而達之天下
===
無不宜反身而誠而達之天下無不順也順理
淵微初無形象今天地人物無不協應昭然可
見非大順之實乎吁先王大順之實著于天地
人物之間其功至此已極矣抑考上文四體既
正以下極言大順之事也故事大積焉而不苑
以下極言大順之理也故禮之大同以下又言
順道之應也至此又極言其大順之實中庸所
謂致中和天地位焉萬物育焉即此意矣有天
下者其可忽諸
